title: Hagar in the wilderness (Genesis 21:8–21)
hookLine: cast out with her son, Hagar sits a bowshot away, and God opens her eyes to a well

lines: A FEAST, AND A LAUGH THAT CUTS.
BREAD, A SKIN OF WATER, THE DESERT.
cards: The laughter doesn't last long in Abraham's tent. At the feast for Isaac's weaning, Sarah sees Ishmael, Hagar's son, mocking, the King James says; other translations say laughing, or playing.
She says to Abraham: cast out this bondwoman and her son. The text says the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight, because of his son.

But God tells him to listen to Sarah, and promises that Ishmael too will become a nation. So early in the morning, Abraham gives Hagar some bread and a skin of water, puts it on her shoulder, and sends them away.

teach.b: Hagar wanders in the wilderness of Beersheba until the water runs out. Then comes the hardest picture in her story.
She puts the boy under a bush, and in the King James Bible: "she went, and sat her down over against him a good way off, as it were a bowshot: for she said, Let me not see the death of the child."
A bowshot: close enough to be near him, far enough not to watch. And she lifts up her voice and weeps. But listen to what the next verse says: "And God heard the voice of the lad."
Remember his name from the first time Hagar ran? Ishmael, God hears. The name comes true again.
The angel of God calls to her out of heaven: what aileth thee, Hagar? fear not. Get up, lift the boy, hold him by the hand. And then: "And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water."
The text doesn't say God made a well appear. It says God opened her eyes.
Was it there all along, a bowshot away, and grief had kept her from seeing it?

teach.h: GOD HEARD THE VOICE OF THE LAD.
teach.b: The text doesn't settle it, but some readers hear it that way.
She fills the skin and gives the boy a drink. The story ends with this: "God was with the lad." He grows up in the wilderness, becomes an archer, and his mother finds him a wife from Egypt.
The household had sent them away. God had not.

teach.h: AND SHE SAW A WELL OF WATER.
teach.b: Muslims remember Hagar and Ishmael too, and tell their own story of her search for water. In Genesis, it ends at a well she hadn't seen.

how: Many Christians turn to Hagar's story in times of exile, abandonment or single parenthood, and some churches and ministries for women and refugees take her well as a sign that God sees and provides.

o: God hears: the name of Hagar's son
he laughs: Abraham's son born to Sarah
God sees: the name of a desert well

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: bread and a skin of water
how far Hagar sat from her son

s: the text says God made a new well appear
it says "God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water."
"and God heard the voice of the lad," as his name, Ishmael, promised.
after the well, God leaves the boy to fend for himself
"God was with the lad," and he grew up in the wilderness, an archer.

games.q: you're Hagar. the water is gone. you've put your son under a bush and sat down a bowshot away, weeping. what happens next?
o: God hears the boy, calls to you, and opens your eyes to a well.
you walk back to Abraham's tent.
games.why: "and God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water." maybe the well was there all along.

practice: Think of a place where you feel the water's run out, money, energy, patience, hope, and notice where you've sat down a bowshot away.
Then look slowly around it, as if your eyes could be opened: a person who's offered, a rest you haven't taken. If you pray, you can ask for your eyes to be opened.

wordCard.voice: Ishmael. Hebrew for God hears: the name that comes true when God hears the boy's cries in the wilderness and Hagar's eyes are opened.

orig.note: Hebrew: a well, as in Beersheba, the wilderness where Hagar wandered.

carryVoice: Your line: there's a well. Sometimes it's closer than grief lets you see. See you tomorrow.
